analysis.one_liner: Creates federal privacy rules for companies handling personal data and strengthens online privacy for children and teens.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced in February 2015 with two cosponsors, it sat in a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee until the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created the first general federal privacy rules for companies that collect personal data on more than 5,000 people. The Federal Trade Commission would write rules requiring companies to secure that data, tell people how it is used, get their opt-in consent for third-party tracking and advertising, collect only what is needed, and notify them and law enforcement after a data breach, with free credit reports for breach victims. A second title, the Do Not Track Kids Act, would extend children's online privacy law to mobile apps, restrict targeted marketing to kids and teens under 16, protect children's location data, and require an "eraser button" so minors can delete their own content. It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to a subcommittee, and no vote was ever taken.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers whose personal data is collected online and off would gain notice, consent, correction, and deletion rights and a right to free credit reports after a breach. Parents and children would gain new protections against apps and websites that collect kids' personal and location data or market to minors. State attorneys general and the FTC would gain new enforcement tools with civil penalties.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers, breach victims, and kids online

how_it_helps.text: The FTC would have to write rules requiring any company holding data on more than 5,000 people to carry out security measures to protect personally identifiable information, with requirements scaled to the size and sensitivity of the data.

Companies would have to clearly disclose how they collect, use, and share personal data, give advance notice of material changes, and offer a clear opt-in consent mechanism for any use that would otherwise be unauthorized, including third-party behavioral advertising.

The bill would require data minimization: companies could collect and retain only the personal information reasonably necessary for a transaction, service, fraud prevention, or similar purpose, and only for as long as needed.

After a security breach, companies would have to notify affected individuals, the FTC, and, for large breaches, a Department of Homeland Security-designated entity that relays notice to the FBI, Secret Service, and state attorneys general; affected individuals would be entitled to free credit reports for two years.

The children's title would apply COPPA's rules to mobile and online apps, require verifiable parental consent for collecting kids' data, bar targeted marketing to children and minors under 16 without consent, protect children's geolocation information, and require an eraser mechanism for content minors post.

Enforcement would sit with the FTC, the Justice Department, and state attorneys general, with civil penalties of up to $33,000 per day or per violation for reckless or repeated violations, adjusted for inflation.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that collect, use, or store personal data on more than 5,000 people each year — data brokers, advertising networks, websites, app makers, and common carriers — would bear the cost of security programs, consent mechanisms, breach notifications, free credit reports for breach victims, and potential FTC, Justice Department, and state penalties. Small businesses and small nonprofits could seek waivers or modified compliance for the credit-report obligation, and banks and health companies already regulated under other privacy laws would be exempt.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data brokers, ad networks, and app makers

drawbacks.text: The bill would preempt state privacy laws covering the collection, use, and disclosure of personal data, wiping out stronger state protections (such as California's) and replacing them with a single federal floor that could be weaker.

It expressly provides no private right of action, so individuals could not sue companies that misuse their data; only the FTC, the Justice Department, and state attorneys general could enforce the rules.

Companies could join FTC-approved 'safe harbor' programs run by private, nongovernmental organizations and be exempted from the bill's notice, consent, and data-minimization requirements, building industry self-regulation into the enforcement system.

Breach notification has large loopholes: a company could exempt itself by concluding there is no reasonable risk of identity theft or fraud, credit reporting agencies must be notified before individuals in some cases, and law enforcement can delay or block public notice.

Penalties are capped — no more than $6 million for a related series of violations and up to $3 million per breach (doubled if reckless or repeated) — sums that are small relative to the revenues of the largest data companies.

The 'unauthorized use' definition carves out broad exceptions, letting companies use personal data for first-party marketing, internal operations, website analytics, and product research without consent.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have given Americans their first general federal commercial privacy law — security duties, consent rights, data minimization, breach notification, and much stronger protections for children and teens — at real compliance cost to the data industry. But it was written to be palatable to that industry: it preempts stronger state laws, bars individuals from suing, caps penalties at levels big companies can absorb, and lets firms opt out of core requirements through industry-run safe harbors. As a package it is a genuine, if diluted, gain for ordinary people over a status quo the bill's own findings describe as inadequate self-regulation — though its death left the stronger state-law patchwork intact, which some privacy advocates would prefer to this federal floor.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade Subcommittee in its first week, and it sat there until the 114th Congress ended, never getting a committee or floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Sires introduced the bill on February 24, 2015, as the Commercial Privacy Bill of Rights Act of 2015 combined with the Do Not Track Kids Act of 2015.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and on February 27 it was sent to that committee's Subcommittee on Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade.
No further action was ever taken: there was no subcommittee markup, no committee vote, no floor vote, and no Senate companion action recorded before the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
The bill attracted only two cosponsors, both Democrats, and never moved out of committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers, advertising networks, and internet platforms that profit from collecting and selling personal data are better off: they kept operating under industry self-regulation and a state-by-state patchwork, with no federal consent, minimization, or breach-notification duties. Consumers, breach victims, and children gained nothing from the bill's death.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll-call record exists; the bill's only support was one Democratic sponsor and two Democratic cosponsors, and the Republican-led committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would force opt-in consent before third-party behavioral advertising, bar re-identifying 'anonymized' data without consent, and limit collection and retention to what is reasonably necessary — direct limits on a business model built on compiling and selling personal profiles. The bill's death left that model untouched.

industries.industry: Internet platforms, websites, and app makers
industries.note: Covered entities holding data on more than 5,000 people would face security, notice, consent, and breach-notification duties and penalties for reckless or repeated violations, and the children's title would extend COPPA to mobile and online apps and restrict marketing to users under 16. Compliance costs fall hardest on firms whose revenue depends on tracking users.

The bill would create FTC-approved 'safe harbor' programs administered by nongovernmental organizations, letting participating companies substitute the program's rules for the bill's notice, consent, and minimization requirements — a new institutional role for industry-run bodies, though only if their standards are substantially as protective as the statute.

They would have to coordinate with companies' breach notifications and provide free credit reports to breach victims for two years, adding obligations, but they would also receive advance notice of breaches before affected individuals in some cases.

Financial institutions regulated under Gramm-Leach-Bliley and health entities under HIPAA would be deemed compliant if they follow their existing regulators' rules, keeping data privacy for money and health under industry-familiar regimes rather than the new FTC framework.
